Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's campaign committee reported owing $2.3 million in debt at the end of March. That creditor is Penn, Schoen & Berland, a political consulting and polling firm that advised Clinton during her presidential bid. The firm's president, Mark Penn, was Clinton's senior campaign strategist until he stepped down last April amid revelations that he had lobbied on behalf of Colombia for a U.S.-Colombia trade deal that Clinton opposed. Penn remained involved with the campaign. Earlier this year, Clinton and her supporters raced to pay as much of the debt as possible by the time she was confirmed and sworn in as the nation's 67th secretary of state on January 21. Kirsten Gillibrand, who was appointed to fill Clinton's seat; and New York congressional candidate Scott Murphy, who hopes to succeed Gillibrand in the U.S. House.

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- On Wednesday, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton hit a significant marker in her effort to eliminate the debt left over from her unsuccessful 2008 White House campaign. For the first time in eight months, her campaign committee reported holding more cash than it currently owes.

While most citizens across the country were busy submitting their federal tax returns, Clinton's campaign committee turned in its financial paperwork to the Federal Election Commission. The filing showed that, as of the end of March, the committee carried $2.3 million in debts while holding $2.6 million in the bank.

Ever since she halted her presidential run in June 2008, the country's chief diplomat has been gradually reducing her outstanding campaign expenses. At that time, her debt had climbed to its highest point of $25.2 million. That figure included $12 million she owed to various vendors, plus $13.2 million she had personally lent to her own campaign.

By the time Democrats gathered for their national convention in Denver, Colorado, last August, Clinton's campaign still had not managed to repay that personal loan. Since the 2002 McCain-Feingold campaign finance law set the convention as the deadline for such repayment, the former New York senator had no choice but to write off the full amount she had loaned.

The debt figures continued to fall over the following months. By the close of November, her campaign owed $6.4 million spread among 16 creditors; by the end of December, that had dropped to $5.9 million owed to five creditors; and by the end of March, only $2.3 million remained, all of it owed to a single creditor.

That remaining creditor is Penn, Schoen & Berland, a firm specializing in political consulting and polling that provided advice to Clinton throughout her presidential campaign. The company's president, Mark Penn, served as Clinton's top campaign strategist until his departure last April. He resigned after it came to light that he had lobbied on Colombia's behalf to promote a U.S.-Colombia trade agreement -- one that Clinton herself had opposed. Even so, Penn continued to stay connected with the campaign.

Earlier in the year, Clinton and those who backed her scrambled to retire as much of the debt as they could before she was confirmed and took her oath as the nation's 67th secretary of state on January 21. From that day forward, Clinton fell under a federal statute called the Hatch Act, which bars federal workers from personally requesting or receiving political donations. However, the same law permits other people to keep raising funds on Clinton's behalf, so long as she is not directly involved.

This week, James Carville -- a longtime Clinton associate and CNN contributor -- distributed a fundraising email to Democrats on behalf of Clinton's campaign. The message asked for donations as small as $5, offering donors a chance to win various prizes, one of which was a day spent with former President Bill Clinton. "I won't spend a lot of time trying to convince you to help Hillary," Carville wrote. "I know what she means to you, and I'm sure you know how important it is for her to have her campaign pay off all its obligations."

Whether the campaign intends to apply its $2.6 million in cash toward wiping out the $2.3 million debt anytime soon remains uncertain. The ongoing fundraising efforts suggest that it does not plan to do so. Further operating costs and other expenditures may also arise. Should any surplus funds remain, they could be given to political causes or refunded to those who donated.

According to the report, Clinton's campaign brought in $938,000 in donations during the opening three months of 2009. Beyond conventional fundraising methods, the campaign also earned money by selling or leasing various campaign assets to outside groups. It collected $2.6 million from Clinton's "Friends of Hillary" U.S. Senate campaign committee in exchange for unnamed assets, along with another $2.2 million by renting out its lists of campaign backers.

Several groups paid to rent Clinton's lists, including the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the inaugural committee for then-President-elect Barack Obama, and the William Jefferson Clinton Foundation. Each of these three organizations paid $274,297. Meanwhile, Clinton's political action committee, HillPAC, paid $822,492 to rent the lists.

The Democratic candidates who rented her campaign lists include Arkansas Sen. Blanche Lincoln; Terry McAuliffe, who is running for governor of Virginia and once chaired Clinton's campaign; New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, who was named to take over Clinton's former seat; and Scott Murphy, a New York congressional candidate seeking to replace Gillibrand in the U.S. House.

# How the Clinton Campaign Monetized Its Supporter Lists Through List Rentals

## Introduction

Political campaigns require enormous financial resources, and successful operations often develop multiple revenue streams beyond direct donations. One common but less publicized practice involves campaigns renting access to their supporter and donor lists to other political entities. Hillary Clinton's presidential campaigns, particularly her 2016 run, employed list rental as one method of generating revenue and maintaining relationships within the broader Democratic ecosystem.

## What Is List Rental in Political Fundraising?

List rental is a well-established practice in both commercial and political marketing. When a campaign builds a substantial database of supporters—including email addresses, phone numbers, and donation histories—that data becomes a valuable asset. Other campaigns, candidates, and organizations may pay to send messages to these supporters, hoping to convert them into their own donors or activists.

Importantly, "renting" a list typically means the list owner sends messages on behalf of the renter rather than handing over the raw data. This preserves the original campaign's control over its supporter relationships while monetizing access to that audience.

## The Value of the Clinton List

By the time of her 2016 campaign, Hillary Clinton had assembled one of the most extensive donor and supporter databases in Democratic politics. This resource reflected years of political engagement, including her 2008 presidential run, her tenure as Secretary of State, and the sustained national profile she maintained afterward.

The list's value stemmed from several factors:

- **Scale**: Millions of engaged contacts nationwide
- **Proven donors**: Many contacts had already demonstrated willingness to give
- **Data richness**: Detailed information on giving patterns and engagement levels
- **Brand association**: Messages connected to a prominent national figure

## How the Revenue Model Worked

Democratic candidates, party committees, and allied organizations could arrange to reach Clinton's supporters, typically through email campaigns. In exchange, they compensated the Clinton campaign, generating revenue that could be redirected toward campaign operations.

These arrangements often took the form of:

- **Fee-based rentals**: Direct payment for access to send a specified number of communications
- **List exchanges**: Reciprocal arrangements where campaigns swapped access to their respective audiences
- **Joint fundraising**: Coordinated efforts where multiple entities shared costs and supporter access

## Benefits for the Democratic Ecosystem

The practice offered advantages beyond simple revenue generation. Down-ballot Democratic candidates and smaller organizations often lacked the resources to build large supporter lists independently. Access to a proven national list allowed them to expand their donor bases and reach potential supporters they could not have found otherwise.

For the Clinton campaign, these arrangements served dual purposes: generating income while strengthening ties with other Democratic entities and supporting the party's broader electoral goals.

## Considerations and Criticisms

List rental practices are not without controversy. Some considerations include:

- **Supporter fatigue**: Frequent solicitations from multiple sources can frustrate donors and diminish list value over time
- **Privacy concerns**: Supporters may not anticipate that their information could be used to reach them on behalf of other candidates
- **Transparency questions**: The financial arrangements behind list rentals are often opaque to the average supporter

Campaigns must balance the revenue and relationship benefits against the risk of alienating their most engaged supporters through excessive commercialization of their contact information.

## Conclusion

List rental represented one component of the sophisticated financial operation behind Hillary Clinton's presidential campaigns. By treating its extensive supporter database as a valuable asset, the campaign generated additional revenue while supporting the broader Democratic Party infrastructure. The practice illustrates how modern political campaigns operate as complex financial enterprises, developing diverse revenue streams and leveraging their accumulated resources in multiple ways. While effective, such practices also raise ongoing questions about supporter privacy and the commercialization of political engagement that continue to shape debates about campaign finance and data practices.

# Clinton Nears Finish Line in Long Effort to Retire Campaign Debt

*Secretary of State reaches milestone in paying off obligations from 2008 presidential bid*

After years of steady fundraising and careful financial management, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has reached a significant milestone in retiring the campaign debt that lingered from her hard-fought 2008 presidential primary battle against Barack Obama—an obligation that at one point ballooned into the millions and became an emblem of the campaign's turbulent final months.

The debt, which peaked at more than $20 million in the immediate aftermath of her withdrawal from the race in June 2008, had become one of the more persistent afterlives of a campaign that began as a presumptive coronation and ended in a grinding, state-by-state slog against an insurgent rival.

## The Origins of the Debt

Much of the outstanding money was owed to vendors, consultants, and, notably, to the campaign's own chief strategist, Mark Penn, whose firm Penn, Schoen & Berland was owed millions for polling and strategic services. Penn, a pollster who had worked for Bill Clinton during his presidency, became a lightning rod for criticism as the primary unraveled.

Penn's strategic vision—predicated on an early knockout blow and a message of inevitability and experience—faltered against Obama's superior organization in caucus states and his mastery of the emerging small-dollar, internet-driven fundraising model. Critics inside and outside the campaign faulted Penn for failing to understand delegate math and for a top-heavy approach that emphasized big states over the grassroots.

"The campaign spent enormous sums early and had little to show for it when the long game began," one Democratic strategist familiar with the operation observed at the time. Penn eventually stepped back from his central role in April 2008 amid controversy, though his firm remained among the largest creditors.

## Carville's Loyalty and the Divided Party

If Penn represented the strategic controversies of the campaign, veteran operative James Carville embodied its fierce loyalties. Carville, the Louisiana-born Democratic strategist who helped engineer Bill Clinton's 1992 victory, remained a vocal and combative defender of Hillary Clinton throughout the primary and beyond.

Carville famously did not mince words about those he viewed as having abandoned the Clintons. His pointed remarks about party figures who backed Obama—including a memorable comparison invoking Judas that he directed at New Mexico Governor Bill Richardson—captured the raw feelings that the protracted contest generated within Democratic ranks.

"Politics is a contact sport," Carville has often said, and few embodied that ethos more completely during the 2008 cycle.

## The Slow Climb Out

Retiring campaign debt is notoriously difficult. Donors, energized by the prospect of victory, are far less motivated to write checks to settle old bills for a campaign that fell short. Federal contribution limits further complicate the task, capping how much any single supporter can give toward debt retirement.

Clinton's ascension to Secretary of State under President Obama added additional constraints. Ethics considerations surrounding her cabinet role limited certain fundraising activities and required careful navigation to avoid any appearance of conflicts of interest given her diplomatic responsibilities.

Nevertheless, the effort continued. Obama himself pledged support in helping retire the debt as a gesture of party unity following their reconciliation. Prominent Democratic donors and grassroots supporters alike contributed over the ensuing period, chipping away at the balance through fundraising appeals, events, and the steady work of loyalists who never fully closed the books on 2008.

## A Symbolic Closing

The near-elimination of the debt carries symbolic weight beyond the balance sheet. It represents a formal closing of one of the most consequential primary campaigns in modern Democratic history—one that transformed the party, elevated a new generation of leadership, and ultimately positioned Clinton for her role on the world stage.

For a campaign that reshaped assumptions about gender, experience, and electoral strategy in American politics, the settling of accounts marks a quiet but definitive end to a chapter that once dominated the national conversation.

Whether it also serves as a prologue to future ambitions remains, as always in politics, an open question.
